text.p: - The ministerial council of the European Union gave the go-ahead to a temporary trade deal with Slovenia that will be in force from January until the association agreement with Slovenia is ratified.
The agreement was approved in spite of complaints from the Netherlands that foreign companies like Shell were not allowed to build petrol stations on Slovenian highways.

- The "Spring" parties, comprising the conservative People's Party, centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, which together won 45 out of 90 parliametary seats in an election two weeks ago, have not yet signed a cooperation agreement that would improve their chances of forming a new government.
- A group of 25 parliametary members attended an introductory visit to parliament on Monday, prior to the first session of the new parliament on Thursday.
- Cultural minister Janez Dular gave a presentation on Slovenian cultural policy to the Council of Europe in Strasbourg on Monday.
- A hearing at a Nicosia court dealing with Slovenia's demand to prolong the freeze of assets of former Yugoslavia in a Yugoslav off-shore bank in Cyprus continues this week.
- A majority of employees of troubled shoe factory Peko went on strike on Monday in protest against unpaid salaries.
- Slovenian rightist daily Slovenec may go into bankruptcy as its managers have so far failed to find fresh capital to cover its debts.
